title: One Kingdom Splits in Two
overview: After Solomon dies, his son Rehoboam answers the people's plea for relief with threats, and the nation breaks into a northern kingdom under Jeroboam and a southern kingdom under David's family.

parts.label: A plea for lighter burdens (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: The northern tribes gather at Shechem, an old meeting place in their own territory, and ask Solomon's son to ease the heavy taxes and forced labor his father demanded. Their spokesman Jeroboam had fled to Egypt after a prophet told him he would one day rule most of Israel (chapter 11).

parts.label: Old advisers and young friends (vv. 6-11)
parts.note: Solomon's experienced advisers say that if the king serves the people now, they will serve him for good. His own circle tells him to boast that his little finger is thicker than his father's waist, meaning he will be far tougher, and to promise "scorpions," probably whips tipped with sharp points.

parts.label: The harsh answer and the break (vv. 12-20)
parts.note: Rehoboam repeats the threats, and the writer says the LORD was at work through this to fulfill the prophet Ahijah's word, without excusing the king's choice. "To your tents" was a cry meaning "we are done here," and when the king sends his forced labor chief, the crowd stones him, makes Jeroboam king of the north, and leaves only Judah loyal to David's family.

parts.label: A war called off (vv. 21-24)
parts.note: Rehoboam gathers a large army from Judah and Benjamin to win the north back by force. A prophet named Shemaiah tells them not to fight their own relatives because the split is the LORD's doing, and they go home.

parts.label: Jeroboam's golden calves (vv. 25-30)
parts.note: Afraid that people traveling to the temple in Jerusalem would drift back to Rehoboam, Jeroboam sets up two golden calves at Bethel near his southern border and Dan in the far north. Many scholars think the calves were meant as stands for an unseen God rather than as gods themselves, but his words echo the golden calf story at Mount Sinai, and the writer plainly calls it sin.

parts.label: A new religious system (vv. 31-33)
parts.note: He builds hilltop shrines, appoints priests from outside the tribe of Levi, which was traditionally set apart for that role, and leads worship himself. He also creates a festival one month later than Judah's autumn harvest festival, a date the writer stresses he chose on his own.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to understand the claim that the split was the LORD's doing while Rehoboam and Jeroboam remain fully responsible for their choices, and how divine control and human freedom fit together.
think: When people ask for relief from a burden, what makes it hard for those with power to really listen?
